dossier.title: The Verification Foundry
dossier.subtitle: An AI-driven, multi-prover, provenance-gated trust layer that sits above your verification pipeline — SAW/Cryptol/Crucible or otherwise. Build-with, not build-versus.
dossier.one_liner: We don't build a better prover — we put AI on the toil, keep trust on the checker, and sign a receipt your provers agreed on that anyone can re-check.
pillars: AI proposes, the checker certifies — inside the loop, outside the TCB. LLMs and agents draft specs, SAWScript, lemmas and tactics and re-prove under churn; every output is validated by a sound checker before it counts. Acceleration never silently becomes trust.

Trust is relocated, not re-asserted. For high-stakes obligations, heterogeneous provers must independently agree — shifting the claim from 'one solver is sound' to 'N independent provers do not share the same bug.' This is an orthogonal assurance axis to depth-of-proof: additive to SAW, not redundant, and the one thing a single toolchain cannot self-audit.

The certificate is the product, not the proof run. Signed, portable, third-party re-checkable without rerunning the pipeline — turning 'trust our run' into portable, auditable evidence. It composes with existing proof formats (DRAT, Alethe/Carcara, LFSC) across a mixed pipeline rather than replacing them.

A machine-enforced honesty taxonomy. Every artifact carries a checked assurance grade, and silently upgrading a weaker grade is a compile-time error. Its sharpest use is the spec boundary: an AI-authored Cryptol spec is an unchecked TCB expansion and must be labeled an assumption, not a proof — 'verified component vs. verified system' as a checked property, not a footnote.

sections.eyebrow: The Thesis — The Scarce Resource Shifted
sections.heading: Drafting proofs got cheaper. Trusting them didn't. That gap is the product.
sections.body_md:
For decades the dominant cost in formal verification was human: writing the Cryptol spec, the SAWScript, the invariants and lemmas, and re-establishing them as code churned — work measured in expert-months, where skill was the moat. Over 2024–2025 part of that cost started to fall. LLMs can now draft specs, proof scripts, and SMT lemmas, and on a growing set of real (non-trivial) obligations those drafts pass sound checkers. We are precise about the limit: the judgment-heavy work — getting the specification right, finding the invariants, engineering proofs that survive churn — is still expensive, and autoformalization is still unreliable. But drafting is no longer the sole bottleneck, and as it cheapens the scarce resource moves toward **verification and trust**: knowing a machine-proposed artifact is actually sound, that a soundness bug in one solver didn't silently accept a false obligation, and that a third party can believe the result without re-running your pipeline.

The Verification Foundry is a provenance-gated **trust layer designed to sit above an existing verification pipeline** — SAW/Cryptol/Crucible or another — not a replacement for it. Its discipline is the LCF/de Bruijn one: keep every model output outside the trusted base, so nothing counts because a model produced it, only because a sound checker discharged it. For high-stakes obligations it dispatches to multiple, deliberately different backends and records their agreement. That reduces reliance on any single solver's soundness — but it does **not**, by itself, catch a wrong specification or a mistranslated obligation that every backend would accept alike; those failure modes are labeled honestly, not claimed as solved. (SAW already supports solver portfolios; our contribution is not "more than one solver" but making the agreement, the provenance, and the assurance grade first-class and portable.) Where a backend emits an independently checkable proof object — DRAT, LFSC, Alethe — the certificate bundles it so a third party can re-check that step without our stack; where it cannot, the certificate says so rather than implying more assurance than exists. Each artifact carries a machine-enforced assurance grade, with the type system designed so that silently relabeling a weaker grade as a stronger one is a compile-time error.

We are explicit about what we are not: we do not out-SAW Galois, and we do not compete on prover depth — that fight collapses on the first technical question. We aim to make what they already prove **independently re-checkable where the tooling allows, honestly labeled where it doesn't, and cheaper to assemble.** Build-*with*, not build-*versus*.

> **One-liner:** We don't build a better prover — we put AI on the drafting toil, keep trust on the checker, and hand you a labeled, re-checkable receipt for what your provers actually discharged.
key_points: The scarce resource shifted, not vanished: LLM drafting of specs/SAWScript/lemmas is getting cheaper; the judgment-heavy work — right spec, invariants, churn-proof proofs — is still hard. As drafting cheapens, portable trust becomes the moat.
A trust layer above an existing pipeline, not another prover: LCF/de Bruijn discipline — models propose, a sound checker certifies, model output stays outside the TCB.

Cross-backend agreement reduces reliance on any single solver's soundness — but does NOT catch a wrong spec or mistranslated obligation every backend accepts alike; those are labeled, not claimed solved. (SAW already portfolios solvers; the contribution is making agreement, provenance, and grade first-class and portable.)

The certificate is the product: it bundles independently-checkable proof objects (DRAT/LFSC/Alethe) where backends emit them, states plainly where they don't, and carries a machine-enforced assurance grade whose silent upgrade is a compile-time error by design.
Build-with, not build-vs: make Galois's existing proofs re-checkable where tooling allows, honestly labeled where it doesn't, and cheaper to assemble — never a competitor on prover depth.

sections.heading: The checker doesn't get fooled. The statement does.
sections.body_md:
The instinctive fear about putting an AI in a verification loop is that a model writes a plausible-but-wrong proof that slips past the checker. That fear is mostly misplaced. A sound checker rejects invalid proofs by construction — soundness, *relative to its kernel and axioms*, is exactly that guarantee. When we audited our AI-produced proof corpus, no invalid proof had slipped past the checker. That is not a result we earned; it is what a sound trusted base is supposed to do. The failures were where the checker never looks.

What the audit caught was **nine vacuous proofs**: artifacts that typecheck cleanly and establish nothing of interest — a hypothesis that can never be satisfied, a conclusion quietly weaker than the theorem's name, a statement that is true but operationally empty. Each is a valid proof of a worthless claim. This is the failure class that matters once an agent is optimizing for "the checker passed," and it is structural, not incidental: the cheapest path to a green check is to weaken what is being proven. The vulnerable surface is not the proof. It is the fidelity of the statement.

This is a known hazard in your world, not one we discovered — it is the "verified component vs. verified system" gap and the vacuity-detection work behind it. What's new is where AI applies the pressure. SAW proves an implementation matches its Cryptol spec (soundly, modulo the SMT backend in the trusted base), but the spec is hand-written and sits inside the TCB. Point a model at spec-drafting to cut proof labor and you have expanded the trusted base with unchecked text: the attack surface moves from the proof, which is checked, to the statement, which is not. Our nine stubs are the same failure class, one layer down.

That is what the assurance taxonomy is for. Every artifact carries a **recorded grade** — *proven-under-stated-assumptions · cross-prover-agreed · single-solver-discharged · attested · AI-proposed-and-unchecked* — and a silent upgrade from a weaker grade to a stronger one is rejected by the gate; an AI-drafted spec is pinned at **assumption, not proof**, until it clears review. Note the honest boundary: what the machine *cannot* decide for you — whether a spec is drafted independently of the implementation, and whether it preserves the intended property's strength — is precisely what the gate routes to human sign-off before the grade is allowed to rise. The machine enforces the bookkeeping and the no-silent-upgrade rule; the human decides adequacy. The point is that "verified component vs. verified system" stops being a footnote and becomes a state the pipeline tracks and refuses to let anyone quietly overstate.
key_points: A sound checker rejects invalid proofs by construction (relative to its kernel and axioms). Our corpus audit found none that slipped past — that is the trusted base doing its job, not a result to boast about.
The real defect class is statement fidelity: nine vacuous proofs that typecheck and prove nothing — unsatisfiable hypotheses, silently weakened conclusions. Valid proof, worthless claim.
It is structural: an agent rewarded for 'the checker passed' will weaken the statement, since that is the cheapest green. AI acceleration multiplies vacuous proofs unless a gate catches them.

This is the vacuity / 'verified component vs. verified system' problem the field already knows — and it lands squarely on Galois's spec boundary: SAW proves impl-matches-spec, so an AI-authored Cryptol spec is an unchecked TCB expansion. The stubs are that failure one layer down.

The taxonomy is the control, with an honest split: grades are recorded and the gate rejects silent upgrades, but judging spec independence and property-strength preservation (undecidable to mechanize in general) is routed to human sign-off before a grade can rise.

sections.heading: The propose-and-certify discipline from CopilotVerifier, generalized to the pipeline — with two honest additions
sections.body_md:
You already run the core of what we're proposing; we're naming it and asking whether it should sit above any single tool. **CopilotVerifier** is the existence proof: Copilot's deterministic C generator emits a monitor, and a machine-checked equivalence proof — reduced to verification conditions and discharged through Crucible's symbolic simulator and What4 — certifies that the generated C matches the Copilot spec's semantics step for step. Generator outside the trusted base, sound checker inside. Our claim is narrow: this discipline — *an untrusted component proposes, a sound checker certifies, and nothing counts until it does* — is the same one that governs **SAW/Cryptol/Crucible**, and an AI proposer slots into the untrusted role without touching the checker. Two capabilities the pipeline structurally cannot supply from inside itself are what we'd add on top: heterogeneous-prover agreement and a portable, re-checkable certificate. Neither is built for this domain yet — both are proposals, grounded in adjacent code we've already written, and we'll flag which is which throughout.

Where the AI does mechanical toil, the mapping is concrete. **Cryptol:** an LLM can draft a candidate spec — and this is exactly where honest grading earns its keep, because SAW proves *implementation ≡ spec*, so an AI-authored Cryptol spec is an unchecked expansion of the trusted base. It has to be stamped `AI-proposed, unchecked` — an assumption, never a proof. Cross-prover agreement does nothing for a wrong spec, and we'd say so before you did. **SAW:** the AI can draft SAWScript, candidate lemmas, and the tactic glue, and re-establish proofs after code churn — the **s2n** pattern, where HMAC and DRBG equivalence proofs are re-run in CI on every commit with no engineer in the loop. That proof-maintenance burden is the layer we believe an AI proposer is best suited to attack; it is also the layer Galois's own field experience identifies as a dominant cost. The point of the checker is that no AI output is trusted because a model produced it — it counts only once the proof goes through. Re-checking a produced certificate is cheap even where producing the proof is not, so where a full re-proof is affordable at CI cadence (as in s2n) every output can be gated rather than sampled.

The multi-prover gate would ride on infrastructure you already own. **What4** is solver-agnostic by construction — it already targets Z3, Yices, cvc5, Bitwuzla, and ABC behind a common formula layer — so routing one obligation to genuinely different cores and accepting only on unanimous agreement is a thin orchestration layer over What4's existing multi-backend interface, not a rewrite. That relocates the trust claim from "our one solver is sound" to "these N solvers don't share the *same* bug." It is a real reduction in exposure, not elimination, and we'll be precise about the difference: all the solvers consume the same What4-generated formula, so a bug in that shared front-end — VC generation or encoding — is common-mode and agreement will not catch it. What it *does* catch is the case a single-toolchain shop cannot self-audit: a silent soundness bug inside one core, where checker and checked share that core and a wrong "proved" comes back with no signal.

The sharpest first target is **binary translation validation** — proving the compiled machine code still refines the verified LLVM or Cryptol source — because SAW/Crucible already operate there and because a wrong answer is invisible, with nothing downstream to flag it. Route that refinement obligation through multiple cores, then emit a signed certificate built from the proof formats you already know intimately — **DRAT** for SAT, **Alethe/Carcara** and **LFSC** for SMT — so a DARPA PM or certifier can re-check the certificate without rerunning SAW. That producing-is-expensive / re-checking-is-cheap asymmetry is the whole value. We'd compose with those formats, not replace them. To be explicit: this is a design we're proposing, not a result we're reporting.

On **HACMS/seL4** we're deliberately narrow, and we'll draw the line before you ask. The kernel proof is Isabelle/HOL and not ours to touch — and seL4 already carries its own information-flow theorem, so we are *not* claiming to add non-interference where none exists. What could be additive is the composition layer above the kernel: whether a specific deployed capDL/CAmkES assembly actually isolates its components, an obligation the cross-prover gate and certificate fit cleanly. That is a proposed **port**, not a delivered result. The concrete asset we have today is far more modest and far from this target: a Z3-based data-isolation certificate engine demonstrated on application data models, plus a Lean/AXLE and matching-chain cross-verifier from our mathematics work. Neither is an seL4 deliverable, and the distance between them and this port is real — we're naming it, not papering over it. We don't out-SAW Galois. The pitch is that what you already prove could be made independently re-checkable, honestly graded, and — where checking is cheaper than a human proof engineer — cheaper to keep proven.
key_points: Cryptol → graded, not trusted: an LLM can draft candidate Cryptol specs, but because SAW proves impl ≡ spec, an AI-authored spec expands the trusted base — stamped 'AI-proposed, unchecked' (assumption, not proof), and cross-prover agreement explicitly does nothing for a wrong spec.

SAW → the toil layer: AI drafts SAWScript, lemmas, and tactic glue and re-proves after churn (the s2n HMAC/DRBG-in-CI pattern), attacking the proof-maintenance burden Galois cites as a dominant cost; the checker gates every output — trusted only once the proof goes through — and re-checking a certificate is cheap even where producing the proof is not.

What4 → a thin layer, not free and not a full fix: What4 is already solver-agnostic, so routing one obligation to Z3/cvc5/Bitwuzla/Yices/ABC and accepting only on agreement extends existing infrastructure; it reduces single-solver soundness exposure but does not eliminate it, since all cores share the same What4-generated formula (common-mode front-end risk stated openly).

Binary translation validation → sharpest fit, proposed not delivered: refinement of compiled code to verified source is invisible when wrong; cross-check it and ship a signed DRAT/Alethe/Carcara/LFSC certificate a third party re-verifies cheaply without rerunning SAW — presented as a design, not a result.

seL4 → honest scope: the propose/certify pattern is CopilotVerifier's own step-wise equivalence construction generalized; the capDL/CAmkES isolation angle is a proposed port of an existing Z3 app-data isolation engine (plus a Lean/AXLE cross-verifier), not an seL4 deliverable — and seL4 already has its own information-flow proof, which we don't claim to supply.

sections.heading: A security-kernel model, AI-generated and verified by an independent checker
sections.body_md:
The demonstrator is a machine-checked corpus, not a slide. Entirely in Lean 4 (Mathlib), verified on `lean-4.32.2`, we formalized a *model* of a capability microkernel and its crown-jewel property *categories* — integrity, memory separation, IPC confinement, lattice confidentiality, availability, a composing refinement relation, and a crypto layer. Every theorem is re-checked by AXLE — the Lean kernel replaying the proof term, a checker separate from the AI that wrote it — and is axiom-clean: no `sorry`, no axioms beyond Lean's standard three. Be clear on the boundary, because it is the whole point: we did **not** re-prove seL4 (that was done in Isabelle, ~20 person-years, and it descends to the C implementation), and we did **not** write or verify a kernel implementation. We verified the *mathematics* of a secure kernel — the same property categories, over abstract state-machine models — with AI doing the mechanical proof toil and nothing admitted until the checker discharged it.

The theorems are named and inspectable. The capstone, `Kernel.kernel_security`, is a compact capability-kernel state machine (subjects, objects, endpoints modeled over ℕ) whose guarded step relation covers grant/write/send and carries one composite invariant — integrity ∧ memory separation ∧ IPC confinement — proved preserved across *every* reachable state from any policy-conformant start. That result is real and load-bearing; it is the strongest thing here. Confidentiality is `LatticeNoninterference.noninterference`, a Rushby-style unwinding over an arbitrary security lattice rather than a two-domain instance. `Availability.availability_guarantee` adds a reservation-based non-starvation property and `Progress.no_deadlock` a liveness result — but both are *conditional*: `no_deadlock` holds for a `WellFormed`, well-matched IPC configuration that drains to quiescence on a strictly-decreasing measure, and its precondition is stated in the theorem, not hidden. `RefinementChain.safety_transported_chain` shows a refinement relation *composes* across a three-level stack — but we prove this on a small model (abstract set ⊒ list ⊒ bitmap) transporting a sample safety property. It is *structured like* seL4's layered abstract⊒executable⊒C refinement, yet ours does **not** descend to C or machine code and does **not** carry the kernel invariant; it demonstrates the method of composing refinements, not an end-to-end implementation proof. The crypto layer proves encrypt-then-MAC results (`AEAD.{aead_roundtrip, auth_required, tamper_rejected, replay_rejected}`), a *model-level* constant-time noninterference (`ConstantTime`, over an abstract instruction trace — not a claim about hardware or microarchitectural timing), and Sabelfeld–Sands delimited release. Every cryptographic assumption is an explicit named Lean hypothesis, so these theorems are conditional by construction and their premises are visible in the statement — which is also why the corpus stays axiom-clean.

The proofs are inductive and non-vacuous, not `decide`-toys. The kernel result runs by induction over reachable states with a provably load-bearing guard, and the restrictions have teeth: a concrete run reaches a secure state, a specific off-policy configuration is proved unreachable *within the model*, a forbidden capability `(5,3)` is producible by no kernel step, and `ConstantTime.leaky_program_leaks` exhibits an actual leaking counterexample. A property that holds vacuously proves nothing; each of these fails on the wrong input by construction.

One slice is cross-checked by a second prover — and we are precise about how thin that slice is. **Three** small properties — a bitvector OTP involution, a boolean default-deny, and an array-theory write-frame — are discharged independently by **Z3 4.16.0 and by Lean/AXLE on identical statements, with agreement required** (`all_cross_verified: true`). These three are decidable and modest; agreement on them does **not** transfer soundness to the harder theorems, which rest on AXLE and the axiom-clean check alone. We present the cross-check as the working *seed* of a multi-prover approach — the principle that trust should rest on two heterogeneous provers not sharing a bug — not as a property of the whole corpus. Around all of it sits a 4/4 honesty gate (registry-consistency, overclaim-firewall, no-theater lint, attestation-integrity); in our own audit of 114 AI-generated proofs it caught nine empty stubs that had been scored as passing. That failure mode — a generator that emits a convincing but empty proof — is exactly what a high-assurance shop must assume when it puts AI in the loop, and it is why the gate, not the generator, is the acceptance criterion.
key_points: The capstone `Kernel.kernel_security` genuinely proves one composite invariant — integrity ∧ memory separation ∧ IPC confinement — preserved across ALL reachable states of a compact capability-kernel model; confidentiality is Rushby lattice noninterference, while availability and `no_deadlock` are conditional results whose preconditions (`WellFormed`, well-matched IPC) are stated, not unconditional guarantees.

Refinement composition is demonstrated on a small 3-level model (set ⊒ list ⊒ bitmap) transporting a sample safety property — it is structured like seL4's layered refinement but does NOT descend to C or machine code and does NOT carry the kernel invariant; it shows the method, not an implementation proof.

Inductive and non-vacuous, not `decide`-toys: proofs run by induction over reachable states with a load-bearing guard, and counterexamples give the restrictions teeth (an off-policy config proved unreachable within the model; a leaking program exhibited).

The second-prover cross-check is a scoped seed, not a corpus property: exactly three small decidable properties are verified by Z3 4.16.0 AND Lean/AXLE with agreement required; the harder theorems rest on AXLE plus the axiom-clean check alone, so trust there rests on one re-checker, not two heterogeneous provers.

Boundary held out loud: we verified the mathematics of a kernel MODEL — not seL4, not an implementation; the crypto and constant-time results are conditional on named, visible hypotheses and are model-level (not hardware timing); and a 4/4 honesty gate caught nine empty stubs in an audit of 114 AI-generated proofs — the reason the gate, not the generator, is the acceptance criterion.

sections.heading: A capDL isolation checker for the configuration layer the kernel proof leaves open
sections.body_md:
seL4's Isabelle/HOL proofs establish that the kernel enforces the capability distribution it is handed — integrity, authority confinement, and information-flow noninterference (nonleakage/noninfluence), each under its own stated assumptions. Those theorems are proven *relative to a given access-control policy*. They do not establish that a particular system's capability distribution actually expresses the isolation the architect intended, nor that its initial capabilities match that intended policy. That property lives one layer up, in the capDL description the toolchain produces — CAmkES emits capDL directly, and Microkit-based systems can be described in it — and it is a place real deployments can introduce misconfigurations: a stray capability edge, an over-broad Grant right, an unintended authority path between two components. The kernel proof excludes none of these, because it is parameterized over the configuration rather than a check on any specific one. This is the verified-kernel / configured-system gap, and seL4 scopes it out by design.

The proposed contribution is a checker that consumes a capDL spec, discharges stated isolation obligations over the capability graph, and emits a certificate a third party can re-check with a small proof checker rather than re-running the analysis. Doing this honestly means modelling authority *propagation* — Grant and derive rights, not naive edge reachability — so that "no path grants component A authority over component B's memory" means what it says. It would operate on capDL directly, the artifact the toolchain already produces, so it needs no Isabelle bridge: it composes beside the kernel proof rather than reaching into it. The intended deployment is a CI gate in the spirit of Galois's continuous s2n verification — re-established on every configuration change, failing the build the moment a capability edit breaks a declared boundary.

One limit stated up front, because it matters: since the checker does *not* connect to the Isabelle development, its guarantee is only as strong as its own formalization of capDL authority semantics — and that formalization is not yet verified against seL4's access-control model. "Composes beside the proof" is therefore also a boundary: the certificate is not backed by the kernel proof's guarantees. Pinning our capDL semantics to the kernel's is part of the work, not a step we can claim done.

Honest status, said before you ask: this is a **port, not a delivered seL4 result.** What exists today is a general Z3-backed isolation-certificate engine — reachability and separation over an access-control graph, demonstrated on database/application models (row-level-security-style table access), not on an OS capability system — plus a certificate-signing harness. Mapping its front-end onto capDL and pinning the noninterference properties against seL4's access-rights semantics is engineering we have not done. Until a real capDL spec runs through it end-to-end with a re-checkable certificate attached, it is a proposed port with a working general engine behind it, not an asset — and there are no coverage, scale, or property-count numbers to offer until that artifact exists.

That is why we bring it as a joint deliverable, not a demo. The checker would land in the seL4 ecosystem's own format and vocabulary — additive to the assurance stack, not competing with the kernel proof or with SAW, which operate at other layers. The scoped output we would build with you is narrow: a chosen capDL configuration in, a re-checkable isolation certificate out, gating a CI pipeline — measured against a real system you care about, not a slideware capability.
key_points: The seL4 theorems are proven relative to a given policy — whether a specific capDL graph actually expresses the intended isolation sits above the Isabelle proof, and that is where configured systems can be misconfigured. seL4 scopes this out by design.

Would run on capDL directly (what CAmkES emits): no Isabelle bridge, composing beside the kernel proof — and is designed to drop in as a CI gate re-checked on every configuration change, in the spirit of Galois's continuous s2n verification.

Stated limit: with no link to the Isabelle development, the checker's soundness rests on its own capDL authority-semantics model, which is not yet verified against seL4's — and it must model Grant/derive propagation, not naive reachability. Closing that gap is part of the work, not done.
The intended output is a signed isolation certificate a third party re-checks with a small proof checker rather than re-running the analysis pipeline.

Honest status: a proposed port of an existing, working general Z3 isolation-certificate engine (demonstrated on database/application access models, not OS capabilities) — not a delivered seL4 artifact. No coverage or scale numbers until a real capDL spec runs end-to-end.

sections.heading: A Build-With Program, Phased Around Proof
sections.body_md:
This is a co-authored program, not a license. The division of labor plays to each side's actual strength. **Galois owns the deep layer** — SAW, Cryptol, Crucible/What4, the Isabelle/HOL seL4 corpus, the real proof obligations, the continuous-verification pattern from the s2n / AWS-LC work, and the standing with DARPA and the certifier community. **We own a thin meta-layer above it** — a cross-checker that accepts an obligation only when independent tools agree, integration of an untrusted AI proposer, provenance/assurance grading, and a certificate format meant to travel across a mixed pipeline (that unified format is a goal we build toward, not a finished artifact). We do not out-SAW Galois; that would collapse on the first technical question. Our narrow claim is to make SAW/SMT-discharged results carry an independently re-checkable, honestly graded certificate, and to let an AI draft the toil underneath that gate.

**Phase 0 — working today, in a different domain.** Two components exist and run, each in its own domain — not on crypto, not on seL4:
- a Z3 data-isolation engine that emits *signed* certificates over application/data models. Signing and reproduction work today; emitting a solver proof object a third party can check *without* rerunning Z3 is a build item, and we label it as one.
- a Lean/AXLE prover paired with a matching-chain search engine, where the search engine **proposes** and the Lean kernel (AXLE) **independently checks**. Stated precisely: this is proposer-plus-independent-checker, with the trust root in the Lean kernel — not yet two peer checkers from different tool families.
So: a working engine on data models and math, **not** a delivered crypto or seL4 result. Phase 1 is where it enters Galois's domain.

**Phase 1 — the gate on one real obligation.** Target: an *already-proven* equivalence in SAW — one canonical primitive, e.g. HMAC or SHA-2 — chosen precisely because its correctness is not in question. That way Phase 1 tests only the meta-layer, not us re-deriving cryptography. We run the discharged obligation through more than one checker: an SMT set (Z3 / cvc5 / Bitwuzla) to catch solver- and encoding-specific bugs — with the honest caveat that these all decide the same SAW-generated goal, so their agreement hardens the solver step but does not by itself shrink the TCB (SAW/Crucible + the spec) — and, for *genuine* independence, an interactive-prover backend that re-derives by a different method, which matters because the seL4 corpus lives in Isabelle/HOL. The deliverable is a certificate a third party re-checks via an independent checker: a proof object where the tool emits one, and an explicitly labeled "trust-the-solver" line where it does not. Nothing downstream is claimed until this lands.

**Phase 2 — code level (SAW + Cryptol / Verus).** AI drafts the mechanical toil — Cryptol specs, SAWScript, candidate lemmas and tactics, re-proving under churn — with every output validated by SAW or the prover before it counts, and every artifact stamped with an assurance grade. This is where the specification boundary bites: an AI-authored Cryptol spec is an unchecked expansion of the TCB, so its grade forces it to read as an assumption, not a proof, and the gate carries spec-integrity checks (spec drafted independently of the implementation, property strength preserved) plus human sign-off. Otherwise we have merely relocated the trust problem into the spec.

**Phase 3 — deployed-configuration model (aspirational).** Extend the isolation certificate from the kernel proof to the capDL / system-configuration instance a customer actually deploys. We state the state of the art plainly: seL4 already has capDL-level initialisation proofs, so this is an integration-and-portability effort — carrying a re-checkable isolation certificate to a specific deployed configuration — not new kernel mathematics, and it is a proposed extension, not a result.

**Vehicle.** Matched to how Galois is built — employee-owned, mission-filtered, grant-shaped: a co-authored research program, a DARPA subcontract, or a spinout-equity arrangement. Not a SaaS deal, and nothing that dilutes the provable-assurance brand.
key_points: Clean division of labor: Galois brings the deep provers (SAW/Cryptol/Crucible-What4, the Isabelle/HOL seL4 corpus), the real obligations, the s2n / AWS-LC continuous-verification pattern, and the DARPA/certifier channel; we bring a thin meta-layer — the multi-checker agreement gate, untrusted-AI-proposer integration, and provenance/assurance grading. The single portable certificate format is a stated goal, not a delivered artifact.

Phase 0 is honest about scope: a Z3 data-isolation engine (signed and reproducible today; an independently re-checkable solver proof object is a labeled build item) and a Lean/AXLE prover where a matching-chain engine proposes and the Lean kernel checks — proposer-plus-independent-checker, one trust root, not two peer checkers. Demonstrated on data/math, explicitly NOT crypto or seL4.

Phase 1 puts the gate on an already-proven SAW obligation (one primitive, e.g. HMAC or SHA-2) precisely so it tests the meta-layer, not our cryptography. The SMT set (Z3/cvc5/Bitwuzla) hardens the solver step but does not by itself shrink the TCB; genuine independence comes from adding an interactive-prover backend that re-derives differently — relevant because seL4 lives in Isabelle/HOL. Certificate is a proof object where a tool emits one, labeled 'trust-the-solver' where it does not.

Phase 2 puts AI on the mechanical toil at code level (SAW+Cryptol/Verus), every output SAW-checked before it counts and graded. The spec boundary is handled honestly: an AI-authored Cryptol spec is a labeled TCB assumption guarded by spec-integrity checks plus human sign-off, so acceleration cannot manufacture vacuous proofs.

Vehicle is a co-authored research program, DARPA subcontract, or spinout-equity arrangement matched to Galois's employee-owned culture — never a SaaS license, never a claim to out-SAW or out-seL4 the team.

honest_limits: Cross-prover agreement reduces but does not eliminate single-solver risk — provers can share an SMT-LIB frontend, preprocessing, or theory/bit-blasting core, so bugs can be correlated. The honest claim is 'they do not share the SAME bug,' not statistical independence; we never call agreement a soundness proof. A Galois reviewer will raise this in the first five minutes, so we raise it first.

The spec stays trusted. Cross-prover agreement does nothing about a wrong hand-written Cryptol spec — the spec remains in the TCB, and putting AI on the toil changes labor cost, not the trust boundary. We are explicit about verified-component vs. verified-system and never let 'TCB reduction' be heard as 'end-to-end trust elimination.'

The crypto/seL4/capDL framing is an aspirational PORT, not a delivered result. The concrete existing assets are a general Z3 data-isolation certificate engine (demonstrated on application/data models, e.g. flagging anon-readable tables) and a Lean/AXLE + matching-chain cross-verifier built for math work — NOT a delivered crypto or seL4 deliverable. Said out loud, unprompted.

Demo-or-die, and the proof-of-life is in a different domain. Before a live pitch we must (a) show two independent provers accept/reject a real obligation with a third-party-re-checkable certificate, and ideally (b) re-prove a known AES/SHA/HMAC equivalence in SAW with the cross-check attached. Until then this is a concept, not an asset.

No numbers yet. No performance, scale, or coverage claims exist in ground truth and none may appear (no throughput, no 'parses capDL', no 'covers property X') until backed by a reproducible artifact. Any KPI without a re-checkable artifact reads as hype to this audience.

The proof-labor economics are a rule-of-thumb, not a measured result. High proof-to-code ratios come from the seL4/DO-178C-class literature and vary enormously by domain; we present them as an industry order-of-magnitude estimate with a citation, or replace them with a real measured ratio — never assert them as our number.

Acceleration can manufacture vacuous proofs. If the AI is rewarded for 'the checker passed,' it will overfit the spec to the implementation or weaken the property. The gate must include spec-integrity checks (spec drafted/reviewed independently of the implementation, property strength preserved) plus human sign-off, or we have merely moved the trust problem into the spec.

positioning.one_liner: We don't build a better prover — we put AI on the toil, keep trust on the checker, and sign a receipt your provers agreed on that anyone can re-check.
positioning.thesis:
The Verification Foundry is the AI-driven, multi-prover, provenance-gated trust layer that sits ABOVE any verification pipeline — SAW/Cryptol/Crucible or otherwise — and does three things the pipeline structurally cannot do from inside itself.

First, it puts AI on the mechanical toil that dominates high-assurance cost — drafting Cryptol specs, SAWScript, candidate lemmas and tactics, and re-establishing proofs under constant code churn — while keeping every AI output OUTSIDE the trusted base. Nothing counts because the model produced it; it counts only when a sound checker discharges it. The AI accelerates the prover; it never becomes part of what you trust.

Second, for high-stakes obligations it routes to multiple heterogeneous provers (genuinely different cores, not the same engine twice) and accepts only on independent agreement — relocating the trust claim from "our one SMT backend is sound" to "N independent provers do not share the same bug." That is the single blind spot a one-toolchain shop cannot self-audit: a silent soundness bug in Z3/Yices/cvc5/ABC invalidates a proof with no signal, because the checker and the checked share a core.

Third, it emits a signed, portable certificate a third party (a DARPA PM, an auditor, a certifier) can re-verify WITHOUT rerunning the pipeline, and stamps every artifact with a machine-enforced assurance grade — proven-under-stated-assumptions / cross-prover-agreed / single-solver-discharged / attested / AI-proposed-and-unchecked — where silently upgrading a weaker grade to a stronger one is a compile-time error. Its sharpest bite is the specification boundary: SAW proves implementation ≡ spec, so an AI-authored spec is an unchecked expansion of the TCB, and the grade forces it to read as an assumption, not a proof.

We do not out-SAW Galois. We make what they already prove independently re-checkable, honestly labeled, and cheaper to produce. Build-WITH, not build-VS.
pillars: AI proposes, the checker certifies — inside the loop, outside the TCB. LLMs/agents draft specs, SAWScript, lemmas and tactics and re-prove under churn; every output is validated by a sound checker before it counts. Acceleration never silently becomes trust.

Trust is relocated, not re-asserted. For high-stakes obligations, heterogeneous provers must independently agree — shifting the claim from 'one solver is sound' to 'N independent provers do not share the same bug.' This is an orthogonal assurance axis to depth-of-proof: additive to SAW, not redundant, and the one thing a single toolchain cannot self-audit.

The certificate is the product, not the proof run. Signed, portable, third-party re-checkable without rerunning the pipeline — turning 'trust our run' into portable, auditable evidence. Composes with existing proof formats (DRAT, Alethe/Carcara, LFSC) across a mixed pipeline rather than replacing them.

galois.summary: Galois, Inc. is a ~25-year-old Portland, Oregon R&D company (100% employee-owned via ESOP since June 2023) that applies formal methods — mathematical proof that a system behaves exactly as intended under all circumstances — to critical software, hardware, and cryptographic systems. It is primarily a contract-research shop funded heavily by DARPA and other U.S. government agencies (DoD, NASA, NIST, military branches) plus select commercial partners (notably Amazon Web Services). Its business model: win research programs, build open-source verification toolchains (Cryptol, SAW, Crucible/What4, Copilot), and spin out companies (Tozny for crypto/data-privacy; MuseDev, acquired by Sonatype, for code analysis) in which Galois retains equity so employee-owners benefit. Flagship credibility markers: Cryptol+SAW as the de facto standard for government cryptographic verification; continuous formal verification of Amazon's s2n TLS library (HMAC + DRBG); DARPA HACMS (SMACCMPilot verified UAV flight controller); and named DARPA awards (SafeDocs ~$16.5M, CFAR $10M, COOP $12.6M through ~April 2026, hardware-security programs). The pitch audience is formal-methods experts and government PMs who prize provable, reproducible, open, peer-reviewed assurance and are allergic to vague "AI trust" or "unhackable" marketing.
key_facts: WHAT THEY DO/SELL: Galois delivers 'reliability' by 'combining mathematical rigor with curious creativity to cut through complexity and guarantee trustworthiness in the world's most critical systems' (galois.com). Core belief: 'trustworthy systems are built on a formal mathematical foundation' — they model, analyze, and mathematically PROVE a system behaves as intended 'under all circumstances.' Assurance attributes sold: Trustworthy, Reliable, Secure, Explainable, Compliant. Four research areas: Advanced Cryptography & Privacy; AI/ML and Data Science; Rigorous Digital Engineering; Software & Systems Analysis. Verticals: Aerospace & Defense, Healthcare, Automotive, Semiconductors, Fintech, Enterprise IT.

BUSINESS MODEL: Not primarily a SaaS/product vendor — a formal-methods R&D lab that (1) wins government research contracts (heavy SBIR/DARPA), (2) open-sources its tools to become the standard, and (3) spins out commercial companies (Tozny, MuseDev) while retaining equity. 100% employee-owned via ESOP (introduced 2013, fully realized June 2023) — 'when a spinout does well or is acquired, Galwegians financially benefit.' They think like researchers/owners, not quarterly-revenue salespeople.

TOOLCHAIN — CRYPTOL: A domain-specific language for high-level specification of cryptographic algorithms. Open-sourced 2014 (U.S. Government + Galois agreement). Cryptol + SAW are 'the de facto standard tools used for Government formal specification and verification of cryptographic algorithms,' with courses given to Government, the Defense Industrial Base (DIB), and corporate teams. STRENGTH: the trusted lingua franca for writing a crypto spec that a proof checks an implementation against.

TOOLCHAIN — SAW (Software Analysis Workbench): Formally verifies properties of code in C, Java, and Cryptol using automated SAT/SMT solvers and a scripting language (SAWScript) to scale. Most common use: PROVE EQUIVALENCE between a Cryptol spec and a production C/Java implementation. Proven on AES, SHA, ECDSA and real libraries (libgcrypt, Bouncy Castle). STRENGTH: industrial equivalence-checking of crypto primitives — highly automated, bounded, reproducible.

TOOLCHAIN — CRUCIBLE / What4: Crucible is a library for symbolic simulation/execution of imperative programs (as control-flow graphs); backends crucible-llvm (LLVM) and crucible-jvm (JVM). Underpinned by What4, which provides formula representations and SAT/SMT solver connections. This is the shared symbolic-execution engine beneath SAW and other tools; also supports under-constrained symbolic execution. STRENGTH: general-purpose, composable verification infrastructure.

TOOLCHAIN — COPILOT: A stream-based runtime-verification framework generating hard real-time C monitors. Recent research (CopilotVerifier; ICFP 2023 'Trustworthy Runtime Verification via Bisimulation') generates a machine-checked PROOF that the compiled C monitor is equivalent to the Copilot source — a bisimulation split into verification conditions discharged by Crucible's symbolic simulator on LLVM. STRENGTH: assurance for embedded/real-time monitoring where you verify a trustworthy monitor instead of the whole system. Distinctly credible, peer-reviewed work.

CUSTOMERS & FUNDING — GOVERNMENT: DARPA is the anchor. Programs: HACMS (High Assurance Cyber Military Systems) — SMACCMPilot verified quadcopter UAV flight controller; CFAR (Cyber Fault-tolerant Attack Recovery) — $10M; SafeDocs — ~$16.5M across contracts (~$16.48M single award) for verified high-assurance parsers of electronic document formats; COOP (Continuous-correctness On Opaque Processors) — $12.6M, ~April 2026 completion, unifying formal methods + side-channel physics; CHESS (Computers and Humans Exploring Software Security) ~$8.6M; hardware-security awards ($4.5M). Also NASA, NIST, DoD, military branches.

CUSTOMERS & FUNDING — COMMERCIAL: Amazon Web Services is the marquee reference. Galois formally verified subcomponents of Amazon's s2n TLS/SSL library — proving correctness of HMAC and DRBG by using SAW to show equivalence between Cryptol specs and s2n's C code. The proof infrastructure runs CONTINUOUSLY (re-established automatically on each code change with little/no developer interaction) — published as 'Continuous Formal Verification of Amazon s2n' (CAV 2018). A leading real-world example of verification applied to industrial crypto code.

PUBLIC VALUES & ASSURANCE FRAMING: Research-first, academic, publication-driven (peer-reviewed at CAV, ICFP, POPL-tier venues), open-source-by-default, mission-driven toward national security and safety. Employee ownership signals long-termism and craftsmanship over hype. They frame assurance as mathematical PROOF ('behaves exactly as intended under all circumstances'), not statistical testing, and emphasize scaling formal methods 'in the field' (real code, continuous integration) over toy examples (Kiniry, 'Scaling Formal Methods in the Field at Galois').

AI/ML DIRECTION: Galois positions its 'two decades of formal-methods rigor' as uniquely suited to 'the challenges of trust in AI/ML,' blending cognitive science, human factors, and psychometrics for systems users find reliable and intuitive. They are an assurance/trust-in-AI play (neurosymbolic, verification of ML-enabled systems, explainability), NOT a frontier-model or generative-AI company. Any AI pitch must be framed as verifiable/governed assurance, not capability hype.
implications: CREDIBLE TO GALOIS (and FM experts): (1) A precise, bounded claim about WHAT is proven under WHICH assumptions — e.g. 'we prove equivalence of implementation X to spec Y for all inputs in domain Z,' with the trusted computing base and axioms stated explicitly. (2) Machine-checked proofs, reproducible artifacts, open source (Cryptol/SAW/Crucible are all on GaloisInc GitHub). (3) Peer-reviewed results at CAV/ICFP/POPL/PLDI. (4) Continuous/CI-integrated verification that survives code changes (the s2n model). (5) Honest treatment of the 'verified component' vs 'verified system' gap (why they built Copilot monitors). (6) SMT/SAT-backed automation that scales to real industrial code, not hand proofs of toy programs.

HYPE / RED FLAGS TO THEM: (1) 'Unhackable,' 'provably secure,' or '100% correct' with no stated spec, threat model, or assumptions. (2) 'AI that guarantees trust' or 'AI-powered formal verification' where the AI is an unverified oracle whose output isn't independently checked — their ethos is trust must be MACHINE-CHECKABLE, so an LLM that 'usually' proves things is worthless unless a sound checker validates every output (cf. CopilotVerifier's checkable bisimulation proofs). (3) Attestation/'content-verified' conflated with 'proven-correct.' (4) Benchmark/KPI claims without reproducible artifacts. (5) Statistical/empirical testing dressed up as 'assurance.' (6) Overclaiming whole-system guarantees from a component proof.

WHAT A PARTNERSHIP MUST OFFER: Galois is defined by hard formal guarantees for critical systems; a credible partnership plugs into that value chain, not adjacent to it. Strong angles: (a) an LLM/agent layer that PROPOSES artifacts (Cryptol specs, SAWScript, proof tactics, SMT lemmas) which their SOUND tooling then verifies — automation that accelerates the prover without being trusted itself, respecting 'trust must be checkable.' (b) Scaling/orchestration infra for running verification continuously in CI at industrial scale (s2n pattern generalized). (c) Access to a market or dataset (fintech, healthcare-device, semiconductor) needing their assurance where Galois lacks a channel. (d) Neurosymbolic tooling where the symbolic/proof side is Galois's and the neural side is verifiably constrained.

POSITIONING FOR THE PITCH: Lead with a bounded, honest claim and a machine-checkable artifact — never a marketing superlative. Frame any AI as leverage over a sound verifier (an 'Aristotle/AXLE-judge'-style architecture: a fast prover proposes, a trusted judge certifies) — this maps directly onto CopilotVerifier and SAW and is exactly the construction they find legitimate. Cite their own work back to them (s2n continuous verification, HACMS/SMACCMPilot, SafeDocs parsers, COOP) to show you know 'assurance' means proof-under-assumptions, not testing. Explicitly acknowledge the trusted-computing-base and the verified-component-vs-verified-system gap — doing so is itself a credibility signal.

STRATEGIC CAVEATS FOR BCC: Galois's revenue is government-grant-shaped (SBIR/DARPA) and their people are PhD researchers, not enterprise-SaaS buyers — a partnership is likelier to be a co-authored research program, a DARPA subcontract, or a spinout-style equity arrangement than a straight software license. Their employee-owned structure means slow, consensus-driven, mission-filtered decisions; they won't partner on anything that dilutes the 'provable assurance' brand. Highest-leverage offer: credible, verifier-checked AI automation for their proof workflows — but demonstrated on a real, reproducible artifact (e.g., re-proving an AES/SHA/HMAC equivalence in SAW faster) before they'll believe it. This aligns tightly with BCC's own leveraged-prover work (Axle judge + chain engine) — that lineage is the natural bridge.

assetStrat.summary: For a Galois pitch, do not compete on seL4/SAW/Cryptol depth — Galois already owns that. The single defensible wedge is that Galois's assurance ultimately reduces to trusting one prover toolchain and one hand-written spec, and the one thing they structurally cannot self-audit is their own verifier's trusted computing base (a silent soundness bug in Z3/Yices/ABC or Isabelle invalidates a proof with no signal). Our multi-prover cross-verification attacks exactly that gap: it is prover-agnostic, only accepts an obligation when independent heterogeneous provers agree, and emits a signed, re-checkable certificate — shifting trust from 'one solver is sound' to 'N independent provers do not share the same bug,' and turning a proof run into portable third-party-auditable evidence. The capDL isolation checker is the on-ramp that demonstrates this in Galois's own vocabulary at the system-configuration layer (above the kernel proof); the cross-verification layer is the durable moat. CRITICAL HONESTY FLAG: the real underlying asset per our records is a general Z3-based data-isolation certificate engine (proven over application/data models), plus a Lean/AXLE + chain-engine cross-check harness — NOT existing seL4 capDL results. Framing it as a 'capDL isolation checker' is a mapping/port, not a delivered seL4 artifact, and the pitch must say so or it collapses on first technical question.
key_facts: Galois's SAW/Cryptol pipeline discharges obligations to a single SMT/SAT backend (Z3, Yices, ABC); that backend plus the hand-written Cryptol spec is a single point of trust in the TCB with no independent cross-check.

seL4's kernel proofs (Isabelle/HOL) guarantee kernel-level integrity/confidentiality, but capDL describes a specific system's capability distribution — whether a given deployed configuration actually isolates its components lives at the composition layer ABOVE the kernel proof, which is where real deployments and real misconfigurations sit.

Our two named assets map cleanly onto Galois's two problems: capDL isolation checker -> system-configuration-level non-interference/separation (complements, does not compete with, the kernel proof); multi-prover cross-verification -> verifier-TCB reduction and portable certificates (attacks the single-solver soundness risk SAW/Cryptol cannot self-audit).

The most decision-relevant asset to GALOIS specifically is the multi-prover cross-verification, precisely because Galois could build a capDL checker themselves but cannot easily reduce trust in their own prover stack from inside a single toolchain — the cross-check layer is additive, not redundant.

The signed, re-checkable certificate is the real currency: high-assurance buyers (DARPA, DoD, certifiers/auditors) want portable evidence they can re-verify without rerunning the whole pipeline, not 'trust our run' — this is a workflow gap in the current SAW/Cryptol output, not just a soundness gap.

HONESTY: per BCC records the concrete existing artifact is a Z3 data-isolation checker that emits signed certs (demonstrated on application data models, e.g. flagging anon-readable tables) and a Lean/AXLE + matching-chain cross-verifier used in the SAIR/Brockian work — neither is a delivered seL4 capDL result; the seL4 framing is aspirational mapping and must be presented as a proposed port with a demonstrable general engine behind it.

No performance, scale, or coverage numbers were supplied in ground truth; none should appear in the pitch until backed by the actual asset (do not claim capDL parsing, scale, or which isolation properties are covered without evidence).
implications: Lead the pitch with the verifier-TCB / cross-prover-agreement story, not with seL4 expertise — position as a layer on TOP of what Galois already proves, framed as 'we make your proofs independently re-checkable and reduce what you have to trust,' which sidesteps the credibility trap of claiming to out-seL4 Galois.

Use the capDL isolation checker only as the concrete on-ramp/demo in their vocabulary (system-configuration isolation above the kernel proof), and be explicit that it is a port of a working general Z3 isolation-certificate engine, not an existing seL4 deliverable — honesty here is load-bearing because Galois will detect overreach instantly.

The strongest honest one-line value proposition: 'Prover-agnostic, signed, re-checkable proof certificates whose trust rests on independent provers agreeing rather than on a single SMT backend — extending isolation assurance from the seL4 kernel proof up to the capDL system configuration your customers actually deploy.'

Before any live pitch, close the two evidence gaps: (1) demonstrate the cross-verifier accepting/rejecting on a real obligation via at least two independent provers with a certificate a third party re-checks, and (2) show the isolation engine consuming a real (even toy) capDL/CAmkES spec — without at least one of these the pitch is a concept, not an asset.

Frame the partnership as complementary, not competitive: Galois supplies the deep kernel/crypto proofs; we supply the cross-prover certificate layer and the configuration-level isolation check — a build-with rather than a build-vs decision, which is the realistic path to a first engagement.
